Find the area $A$ bounded by the polar curve $r=2\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\theta )$ for $-\frac{\pi }{6}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{6},$ as shown above. Do not round the answer.

$A=$
{{field-1}}
q-348315.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\text{d}\theta ,
$$

where $r(\theta )=2\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\theta )$, ${\theta }_{1}=-\frac{\pi }{6}$ and ${\theta }_{2}=\frac{\pi }{6}.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6}{(2\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\theta ))}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6}{cos}^{2}⁡(3\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6}(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\theta ))\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =(\theta +\frac{1}{6}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6\theta )){|}_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6} \\  & =(\frac{\pi }{6}-(-\frac{\pi }{6}))+\frac{1}{6}(\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi -\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\pi )) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{3}+0 \\  & =\frac{\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-352321.name: Question 6
q-352321.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

When $r(\theta )=3+4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $, ${\theta }_{1}=-\frac{\pi }{3}$ and ${\theta }_{2}=\frac{\pi }{3}$, this gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /3}^{\pi /3}(3+4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /3}^{\pi /3}(9+24\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +16{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /3}^{\pi /3}(9+24\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +8(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )))\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(17\theta +24\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )){|}_{-\pi /3}^{\pi /3} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(17\theta \,{|}_{-\pi /3}^{\pi /3}+24\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{|}_{-\pi /3}^{\pi /3}+4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,{|}_{-\pi /3}^{\pi /3}) \\  & =\frac{17}{2}\theta \,{|}_{-\pi /3}^{\pi /3}+12\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{|}_{-\pi /3}^{\pi /3}+2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,{|}_{-\pi /3}^{\pi /3} \\  & =\frac{17}{2}(\frac{\pi }{3}+\frac{\pi }{3})+12(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})-\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\frac{\pi }{3}))+2(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi }{3})-\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\frac{2\pi }{3})) \\  & =\frac{17\pi }{3}+12(\sqrt{3})+2(\sqrt{3}) \\  & =\frac{17\pi }{3}+14\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 7
?

Which of the following gives the total area enclosed by the graph of the polar curve r=sin⁡θ+2 for π4≤θ≤π?

a
12∫π/4π(cos2⁡θ+4sin⁡θ+4)dθ
b
12∫π/4π(sin2⁡θ+4sin⁡θ+4)dθ
c
12∫π/4π(sin2⁡θ+4)dθ
d
12∫0π(cos2⁡θ+2cos⁡θ+4)dθ
e
12∫π/23π/4(4sin⁡θ+4)2dθ
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The area bounded by a polar curve is given by A=12∫θ1θ2r2(θ)dθ.

When r(θ)=sin⁡θ+2, θ1=π4 and θ2=π, this gives

A=12∫π/4π(sin⁡θ+2)2dθ=12∫π/4π(sin2⁡θ+4sin⁡θ+4)dθ.

q-20640.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14217747/assets/4a83949bcdf4ed8d99cac451d6db21986c24819d1601578890f86fe3df99666a.png)

Find the area bounded by the polar curve $r=2+2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ for $\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \pi ,$ as shown above.
q-20640.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

When $r(\theta )=2+2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $, ${\theta }_{1}=\frac{\pi }{2}$ and ${\theta }_{2}=\pi $, this gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }(2+2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }(4+8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +4{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{4}{2}{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }(1+2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2(\theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi }+2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi }+\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ))\,\text{d}\theta ) \\  & =2(\theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi }+2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi }+\frac{1}{2}(\theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi }+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )}{2}\,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi })) \\  & =2(\theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi }+2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi }+\frac{1}{2}\theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi }+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )}{4}\,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi }) \\  & =3\theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi }+4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi }+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )}{2}\,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi } \\  & =3(\pi -\frac{\pi }{2})+4(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}))+\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )) \\  & =\frac{3\pi }{2}-4+\frac{1}{2}(0) \\  & =\frac{3\pi -8}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Find the area bounded by the polar curve r=2+2cos⁡θ for π2≤θ≤π, as shown above.

a
3π2
b
3π−82
c
3π+82
d
3π+42
e
3π+84
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The area bounded by a polar curve is given by A=12∫θ1θ2r2(θ)dθ.

When r(θ)=2+2cos⁡θ, θ1=π2 and θ2=π, this gives

A=12∫θ1θ2r2dθ=12∫π/2π(2+2cos⁡θ)2dθ=12∫π/2π(4+8cos⁡θ+4cos2⁡θ)dθ=42∫π/2π(1+2cos⁡θ+cos2⁡θ)dθ=2(θ|π/2π+2sin⁡θ|π/2π+12∫π/2π(1+cos⁡(2θ))dθ)=2(θ|π/2π+2sin⁡θ|π/2π+12(θ|π/2π+sin⁡(2θ)2|π/2π))=2(θ|π/2π+2sin⁡θ|π/2π+12θ|π/2π+sin⁡(2θ)4|π/2π)=3θ|π/2π+4sin⁡θ|π/2π+sin⁡(2θ)2|π/2π=3(π−π2)+4(sin⁡(π)−sin⁡(π2))+12(sin⁡(2π)−sin⁡(π))=3π2−4+12(0)=3π−82.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14217747/assets/ed702f9d982d599fc0f175dc7d7dd022aeefc3f5463aade2a9db71313faf4866.png)

Find the area bounded by the polar curve $r=1+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ for $0\le \theta \le \pi ,$ as shown above.
q-9641.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

When $r(\theta )=1+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $, ${\theta }_{1}=0$ and ${\theta }_{2}=\pi $, this gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1+2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi }+2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi }+\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ))\,\text{d}\theta ) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi }+2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi }+\frac{1}{2}(\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi }+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,{|}_{0}^{\pi })) \\  & =\frac{3}{4}\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi }+\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi }+\frac{1}{8}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,{|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =\frac{3}{4}(\pi -0)+(\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi -\operatorname{sin}⁡0)+\frac{1}{8}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡0) \\  & =\frac{3\pi }{4}+0+\frac{1}{8}(0) \\  & =\frac{3\pi }{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Find the area bounded by the polar curve $r=3-3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ for $\frac{3\pi }{2}\le \theta \le 2\pi ,$ as shown above.
q-123912.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

When $r(\theta )=3-3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $, ${\theta }_{1}=\frac{3\pi }{2}$ and ${\theta }_{2}=2\pi $, this gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }(3-3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }(9-18\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +9{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{9}{2}{\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }(1-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{9}{2}(\theta \,{|}_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{|}_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }+\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ))\,\text{d}\theta ) \\  & =\frac{9}{2}(\theta \,{|}_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{|}_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }+\frac{1}{2}(\theta \,{|}_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )}{2}\,{|}_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi })) \\  & =\frac{9}{2}(\theta \,{|}_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{|}_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }+\frac{1}{2}\theta \,{|}_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )}{4}\,{|}_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }) \\  & =\frac{27}{4}\theta \,{|}_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }-9\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{|}_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }+\frac{9\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )}{8}\,{|}_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{27}{4}(2\pi -\frac{3\pi }{2})-9(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2}))+\frac{9}{8}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\pi )) \\  & =\frac{27\pi }{8}-9+\frac{9}{8}(0) \\  & =\frac{27\pi -72}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-352330.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

When $r(\theta )=2\theta $, ${\theta }_{1}=0$ and ${\theta }_{2}=\pi $, this gives

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }(2\theta )^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }4{\theta }^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\theta }^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2(\frac{{\theta }^{3}}{3})\,{|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =2(\frac{{\pi }^{3}}{3})-2(\frac{{0}^{3}}{3}) \\  & =\frac{2{\pi }^{3}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

$A=$
{{field-1}}
q-352331.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

When $r(\theta )=2+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )$, ${\theta }_{1}=0$ and ${\theta }_{2}=\frac{\pi }{2}$, this gives

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(2+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ))^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(4+4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )+{sin}^{2}⁡(2\theta ))\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(4+4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )+\frac{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\theta )}{2})\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(\frac{9}{2}+4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\theta ))\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{9}{2}\theta -2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\theta )}{8}){|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{9\pi }{4}+4) \\  & =2+\frac{9\pi }{8}.\end{aligned}
$$
